la:verb:propono.gloss: to set forth, to put forth, to lay out
senses: to set forth, to put forth, to lay out
la:verb:propono.html:
prō-pōno, pŏsŭi, pŏsĭtum, 3, v. a.,
to put or set forth, to set or lay out, to place before, expose to view, to display (class.).
Lit.: proponere vexillum,: pallentesque manus, sanguineumque caput,: i puer et citus haec aliquā propone columnā,aliquid venale,to expose for sale,; cf. : geminum pugnae proponit honorem,proposes, offers,: singulis diebus ediscendos fastos populo proposuit,: legem in publicum,: in publico epistulam,; : vectigalia,to publish, publicly advertise,: oppida Romanis proposita ad copiam commeatūs,: ne quid volucre proponeretur, praeter, etc.,should be served up, (al. poneretur).—
Trop.
To set before the eyes, to propose mentally; to imagine, conceive: propone tibi duos reges,: aliquid sibi exemplar,: sibi aliquem ad imitandum,: vos ante oculos animosque vestros ... Apronii regnum proponite,: eam (vitam) ante oculos vestros proponite,: condicio supplicii in bello timiditati militis proposita,; ; : vim fortunae animo,: spem libertatis,: nihil ad scribendum,.—
To expose: omnibus telis fortunae proposita est vita nostra,: tabernis apertis proposita omnia in medio vidit,.—
To point out, declare, represent, report, say, relate, set forth, publish, etc. (cf.: indico, denuntio): ut proponat, quid dicturus sit,; : extremum illud est de iis, quae proposueram,: contione habitā, rem gestam proponit,: in exemplum proponere,; .—With de: de Galliae Germaniaeque moribus, et quo differant eae nationes inter se,.—With object-clause: quod ante tacuerat, proponit, esse nonnullos, quorum, etc.,: cui (morbo) remedia celeria faciliaque proponebantur,were proposed, suggested, believed to be efficient,.—
To offer, propose as a reward: Xerxes praemium proposuit, qui invenisset novam voluptatem,: populo congiarium, militi donativum,.—
In a bad sense, to threaten, denounce: cui cum publicatio bonorum, exsilium, mors proponeretur,: injuriae, quae propositae sunt a Catone,, b, 2: contentiones, quae mihi proponuntur,: improbis poenam,: damnationem et mortem sibi proponat ante oculos,; .—
To lay before, to propose for an answer: aliquam quaestionem, Nep : aenigma,.—
To purpose, resolve, intend, design, determine: consecutus id, quod animo proposuerat,: cum id mihi propositum initio non fuisset,I had not proposed it to myself, had not intended it,.— With inf.: neque propositum nobis est hoc loco (laudare), etc.,I am resolved,.—With ut: propositum est, non ut eloquentiam meam perspicias, sed ut,the design is,.—
To say or mention beforehand (post-Aug.), .—
To state the first premise of a syllogism: cum proponimus,; .—
To impose (post-class.): novam mihi propono dicendi legem,.—Hence, prōpŏsĭtum, i, n.
A plan, intention, design, resolution, purpose (class.): quidnam Pompeius propositi aut voluntatis ad dimicandum haberet,: assequi,to attain,: est enim propositum, ut iratum efficiat judicem,: tenere,to keep to one's purpose,; ; ; ; : propositum peragere,: tenax propositi,: in proposito manere. : reprehendendi habere,: omne propositum operis a nobis destinati,; ; .—
The first premise of a syllogism, ; .—
An argument: nam est in proposito finis fides, .—
The main point, principal subject, theme: a proposito declinare aliquantulum,: egredi a proposito ornandi causā,: a proposito aberrare,: redire ad propositum,: ad propositum revertamur,: a proposito aversus,: propositum totius operis,; : vitae,: meum,: tuum,.—
A way, manner, or course of life (poet. and post-Aug.): mutandum tibi propositum est et vitae genus,: vir proposito sanctissimus,.

la:adv:propter.html:
propter, adv. and prep.
contr. for propiter, from prope; cf.: inter, subter
.
Adv., near, hard by, at hand (syn.: prope, juxta; rare but class.). serito in loco, ubi aqua propter siet,: ibi angiportum propter est,: propter dormire,: araque Panchaeos exhalat propter odores,: propter est spelunca, (al. prope): vident unum virum esse ... et eum propter esse,: cum duo reges propter assint,: (caules) si propter sati sunt,: duo filii propter cubantes,; : adulescentia voluptates propter intuens,; id. ap. : cornix propter volans,: praeter propter, v praeter. —
Prep. with acc., near, hard by, close to (syn.: prope, juxta, ad).
Lit., of place (rare but class.); stat propter virum fortem,; ; : partem cohortium propter mare collocat, Sisenn ap. : hic propter hunc assiste,: propter eam porticum situm erat dolium, Varr ap. : propter Platonis statuam consedimus,: propter aliquem assidere, (cited ap. ): insulae propter Siciliam,: propter aquae rivum,; .—Following its case: viam propter,: hostem propter,.—
Trop., in stating a cause.
On account of, by reason of, from, for, because of (syn. ob; the predom. signif. of the word): parere legibus propter metum,; cf.: propter metum poenae,: propter eam ipsam causam,: propter frigora frumenta in agris matura non erant,: propter humanitatem,: is propter morbum exire non potuit,: excusato languore faucium propter quem non adesset,; ; : bidentes propter viam facere, to sacrifice on account of a journey, Laber, ap. ; cf.: propter viam fit sacrificium quod est proficiscendi gratiā, Herculi aut Sanco, Müll.; : propter injuriam,to avoid injury,: propter hoc, propter quod,on that account, for which reason,; : propter me, te, etc., on my, thy account, etc., as far as I (you, etc.) are concerned, = mea causā, or per me: egon propter me illam decipi miseram sinam?; : non est aequom me propter vos decipi,: di numquam propter me de caelo descendent,.—
Through, by means of (rare).
Referring to persons in whom lies the cause of a thing: te propter tuam Matrem non posse habere hanc uxorem domi,: propter quos vivit,through whom he lives, to whom he owes life,: lugere eum, propter quem ceteri laetarentur,; 34, 93.—
To things by means of which any thing takes place: quid enim refert, utrum propter oves, an propter aves fructus capias?.— Placed after its case: quod propter studi, um cum rem neglegere familiarem videretur,; ; : suctum propter lactis,: quam propter tantos potui perferre labores,.

senses: because of, on account of, for, according to

la:verb:propero.html:
prŏpĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.
properus
.
Act., to hasten, quicken, accelerate; to prepare, make, or do with haste (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose): alia quae incepto usui forent properare,: itineris properandi causā,

105, 2: properato itinere,: vascula intus pure propera,: obsonia,: fulmina,: pecuniam heredi,: mortem,; : coeptum iter,: deditionem,: caedem,: naves,: hoc studium,.—In pass.: vellera properabantur,: teneri properentur amores, Dum vacat, let them be sung hastily or briefly, : properatur amor,: hinc porticus, inde delubra properantur,.—

Neutr., to make haste, to hasten, be quick (class.): aliud est properare, aliud festinare. Qui unum quid mature transigit, is properat: qui multa simul incipit neque perficit, is festinat, Cato ap. ; id. ap. Müll.; id. ap. : propera, fer pedem,: properatin' ocius?: simulabat sese negotii causā properare,; : in Italiam,; : ad praedam, ad gloriam,: ad gaudia,: Romam,: in patriam,: in fata,: sacris, for a sacris,; ; but sometimes with collat. notion of excessive haste: properantibus Blaesus advenit, increpabatque, etc. (cf. the context),; .— With sup.: ultro licentiam in vos auctum, atque adjutum properatis, Sall. Or. Licin. ad Pleb. (H. 3, 61, 16 Dietsch).—With inf.: argentum propere propera vomere,: redire in patriam,: quin huc ad vos venire propero?: signa inferre, atque evadere oppido,: pervenire,: aliquem amando Perdere,.—With object-clause: se quisque hostem ferire properabat,; .—Impers. pass.: properatum vehementer, cum, etc.,; .—Transf., of inanimate subjects, with inf. pass.: mala decerpi properantia,.—Hence,
prŏpĕrans, antis, P. a., hastening, hasty, rapid, speedy (class.): ille properans, festinans,: haec properantes scripsimus,in haste,, a.—Comp.: rotam solito properantior urget,.—Hence, adv.: prŏpĕran-ter, hastily, speedily, quickly (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; cf.: propere, cito, festinanter, celeriter, etc.),: properanter accepit codicillos,.—Comp.: beneficia properantius, quam aes mutuum, reddere,; : ire,.—Sup.: properantissime aliquid afferre, Cod. Th. 11, 30, 8.—
prŏpĕrātus, a, um, P. a., hurried, accelerated, rapid, quick, speedy (mostly poet.): tabellae,: mors,: gloria rerum,: meta curribus,i. e. rapidly approached,: naves,: tela,.—Comp.: properatius tempus,.—Absol.: properato opus est, there is need of haste: accurato et properato opus est,: erat nihil, cur properato opus esset,.—Hence, adv.: prŏpĕrā-tō, quickly, speedily (Tac.): properato ad mortem agitur,.
la:verb:propero.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.

la:adj:propior.html:
prŏpĭor, ĭus,
gen. ōris, adj. comp., and proxĭmus, a, um, adj. sup. (v. below, II.) [from the obsol. propis; whence prope].
Comp., nearer, nigher.
Lit., of place: portus propior,: tumulus,: ut propior patriae sit fuga nostra,: domus, Dietsch: cum propior caliginis aër Ater init oculos, (314).—With acc.: propior montem suos collocat,: propior hostem,.—With ab: quisquis ab igne propior stetit,.—With inf.: propior timeri,.—Neutr. plur, subst.: prŏpĭōra, um, places lying near: propiora fluminis,: tenere,.—
Trop.
Of time, nearer, later, more recent: veniunt inde ad propiora,: venio ad propiorem (epistulam),: propior puero quam juveni,: septimus octavo jam propior annus,; : mors,: propiore aut longiore tempore aliquid facere,.—
Of relationship, nearer, more nearly related; with dat.: quibus propior P. Quintio nemo est,: ille gradu propior sanguinis,; ; : amicus,.—
Of resemblance, more nearly resembling, more like (class.); with dat.: quae sceleri propiora sunt, quam religioni,: tauro,: vero est propius,more probable,; ; ; : scribere Sermoni propiora,.—With acc. (not in Cic.): propius est fidem,is more credible,: quod tamen vitium propius virtutem erat,.—
Of relation or connection, nearer, more nearly related, affecting or concerning more nearly, of greater import, closer, more intimate: hunc priorem aequom'st me habere: tunica propior pallio est, proverbially,my shirt is nearer than my coat,: propior societas eorum, qui ejusdem civitatis,: sua sibi propiora pericula esse, quam mea,: alium portum propiorem huic aetati videbamus,: damnum propius medullis,: cura propior luctusque domesticus,; : supplemento vel Latium propius esse,: irae quam timori propiorem cernens,more inclined to anger than to fear,: oderat Aenean propior Saturnia Turno, more inclined or attached to, .—Hence, adv.: prŏpĭus, more nearly, nearer, closer (class.).
Lit.
Absol.: propius accedamus,; : res adspicere,: propius spectare aliquid,; stare,.—
With dat., nearer to: propius grammatico accessi, Cic. ap. P. (not elsewhere in Cic.): propius Tiberi quam Thermopylis,: propius stabulis armenta tenerent,.—
With acc.: ne propius se castra moveret,: pars insulae, quae est propius solis occasum,: propius aliquem accedere, : propius urbem,: mare,.—
With ab: propius a terris,: antiquitas quo propius aberat ab ortu et divinā progenie, hoc melius ea cernebat,: ab Urbe,.—
Trop.: ut propius ad ea accedam, quae a te dicta sunt,; ; : propius accedo: nego esse illa testimonia,: a contumeliā quam a laude propius fuerit post Vitellium eligi,: nec quicquam propius est factum, quam ut illum persequeretur,he was within an ace of following him,; so, propius nihil est factum, quam ut occideretur,.
Sup.: proxĭmus (PROXVMVS and PROXSVMEIS, Tab. Bant.; late comp. proximior, ; Ulp. ap. P.; v. below, B. 2. and 3.; cf. in adv. 2. c.), a, um, adj., the nearest, next (class.).
Lit., of place: proxima oppida,: via,; cf.: via ad gloriam proxima et quasi compendiaria,: ad proximum mare, dein Romam pergerent,: in proximos collis discedunt,: proximum iter in Galliam,: paries cum proximus ardet,: agri termini,: proximus vicinus,one's nearest neighbor,; ; ; .—With dat.: Belgae proximi sunt Germanis,: huic proximum inferiorem orbem tenet πυρόεις, : proxima Campano ponti villula,.—With acc. (not in Cic.): qui te proximus est,: ager proximus finem Megalopolitarum,: Crassus proximus mare Oceanum hiemarat,: qui proximi forte tribunal steterant,.—With ab, nearest to, next to: dactylus proximus a postremo,next before,: ut quisque proximus ab oppresso sit,: proximus a dominā,: proxima regio ab eā (urbe),. —Hence, as subst.,
proxĭmus, i, m., a neighbor, a fellow-man, ; .—As subst.,
proxĭmum, i, n., the neighborhood, vicinity: vicinus e proximo,hard by,: aquam hinc de proximo rogabo,from the house next door,: cum in proximo hic sit aegra,close by, next door,: huic locum in proximum conduxi,: per impluvium huc despexi in proximum,into our neighbor's,.—Plur.: traicit in proxima continentis,.—
Trop.
Of time, the next preceding or following, the previous, last, the next, the following, ensuing: quid proximā, quid superiore nocte egeris,: his proximis Nonis, cum in hortos Bruti venissemus,: Gabinius quem proximis superioribus diebus acerrime oppugnasset,: se proximā nocte castra moturum, on the next, i.e. the following night, ; ; ; : proximo anno,; : in proxumum annum (se) transtulit,: proximo, altero, tertio, denique reliquis consecutis diebus,: bello tanto majore quam proximo conatu apparatum est, Weissenb. ad loc.: IN DIEBVS V. PROXSVMEIS QVIBVS QVISQVE EORVM MAG (istratum) INIERIT, Tab. Bantin. lin. 14; so ib. lin. 12; ; : censor qui proximus ante me fuerat,: die proximi, old abl. form for proximo, Cato ap. , and ap. ; cf.: crastinus, pristinus, etc., but proximo a. d. VI. Kal. Octobr.,recently, last of all,.—
In order of succession, rank, estimation, worth, etc., the next: summa necessitudo videtur esse honestatis: huic proxima incolumitatis: tertia ac levissima commoditatis,: observat L. Domitium maxime, me habet proximum,: proximos dentes eiciunt,: prima vulnera ... Proxima,: proximos illi tamen occupavit Pallas honores,: proximum est, ut, it follows that, remains that, the next point is: proximum est ergo, ut, opus fuerit classe necne quaeramus, we must next inquire, : proximum est, ut doceam, deorum providentiā mundum administrari,.—Of value or quality, the next, most nearly approaching, most like or similar: id habendum est antiquissimum et deo proximum, quod est optimum,: ficta voluptatis causā sint proxima veris,: proxima Phoebi Versibus ille facit,.—Comp.: ut quorum abstinentiam interrupi, modum servem et quidem abstinentiae proximiorem,.—
In relationship, connection, or resemblance, the nearest, next, most nearly or closely related, next of kin, most like: AGNATVS PROXIMVS, Fragm. XII. Tabularum: hic illi genere est proximus,: proximus cognatione,: id des proximum,: proxima virtutibus vitia,: propinquitate,: proximae necessitudines,.— Comp.: si quis proximior cognatus nasceretur, Ulp. ap. P.—Subst.: proxĭmi, ōrum, m., one's nearest relatives, next of kin: injuriosi sunt in proximos,; Caes. Fragm. ap. ; : cum haec omnia cumulate tuis proximis plana fecero,i.e. to your friends, intimates,; ; .—
In gen., one's neighbor, fellow-man: sive nostros status, sive proximorum ingenia contemplamur,; : quis est mihi proximus?; Serm. 8, 2; 90, 7 init.—
That is nearest at hand, i. e. apt, fit, suitable, convenient, easy (anteand post-class.): argumentum,: cum obvium proximumque esset dicere, etc.,: eamus ad me; ibi proximum est, ubi mutes,there is the fittest, most convenient place,.—Adv.: proxĭmē (proxume; comp. proximius, v. below, 2. c.), nearest, very near, next.
Lit., of place, with dat. (not in Cic., rare in Livy): quam proxime potest hostium castris castra communit,; .—With acc.: exercitum habere quam proxime hostem,: proxime Pompeium sedebam,: proxime Hispaniam Mauri sunt,.—With ab: a Surā proxime est Philiscum oppidum Parthorum,: omnes tamen quam proxime alter ab altero debent habitare,.—
Trop.
Of time, shortly before or after, last, next: civitates quae proxime bellum fecerant,: Tito fratre suo censore, qui proximus ante me fuerat,; ; : cum proxime judices contrahentur,.—With acc.: proxime abstinentiam sumendus est cibus exiguus,: proxime solis occasum,.—
Of order, rank, estimation, condition, etc., next to, next after, next: proxime et secundum deos homines hominibus maxime utiles esse possunt,: me huic tuae virtuti proxime accedere,: proxime a nobilissimis viris,; : proxime valent cetera lauri genera,: utilissimum esse omphacium; proxime viride,.—With acc.: esse etiam debent proxime hos cari, qui, etc., Cass. ap. : proxime morem Romanum,closely following the Roman method,: erat res minime certamini navali similis, proxime speciem muros oppugnantium navium,closely resembling,.—In this sense also with atque: proxime atque ille aut aeque,nearly the same as he,.—
Very closely, nicely, accurately: ut proxime utriusque differentiam signem, Spald.; cf.: analogia, quam proxime ex Graeco transferentes in Latinum proportionem vocaverunt,. —Comp.: nonne apertius, proximius, verius?.

senses: conduct of life, lifestyle, moral principles

la:adv:prope.html:
prŏpe, adv. and prep.
pro and demonstr suff. -pe (cf.: nempe, quippe), = Sanscr. -pa
.
Adv. (comp. propius, and sup. proxime, v. under propior), near, nigh (class.).
Lit., in space: quaenam vox mihi prope hic sonat? Quis hic loquitur prope?: prope ad aliquem adire,: aedes accedere,: prope alicubi esse,: intueri aliquid (opp. procul),.—
With ab, near to, near by, hard by: bellum tam prope a Siciliā,: prope a meis aedibus,: prope ab domo detineri,.—So, comp.: stellae, aliae propius a terris, etc.,: propius visere mala reipublicae,.—
Transf.
In time, near, not far off: partus instabat prope, was near at hand, Ter Ad. 3, 2, 9.—Esp. with quando, cum, ut, the time is near or not far off, when, etc.: prope est, quando herus pretium exsolvet,: prope adest, quom alieno more vivendum est mihi,: partitudo prope adest, ut fiat palam,; : nox prope diremit colloquium,i. e. the approach of night,; cf. ; .—

etym. dub.; perhaps from root prae; cf. prope
,

(class. and freq.): ut cum ademerit nobis omnia, quae nostra erant propria, ne lucem quoque hanc, quae communis est, eripere cupiat,all that belonged peculiarly to us,: suā quādam propriā, non communi oratorum facultate,: ut redeas ad consuetudinem vel nostram communem vel tuam solius et propriam, Luc. ap. : omnia qui jubet esse communia, ne quis civis propriam aut suam rem ullam queat dicere,; id. ap. : suis propriis periculis parere commune reliquis otium,: quod (periculum) autem meum erat proprium,; ; calamitatem aut propriam suam aut temporum queri,.—

Subst.: prōpătŭlum, i, n., an open or uncovered place.
In phrase in propatulo (class.): in propatulo ac silvestribus locis, in the open air (opp.: domi sub tecto), ap. : in propatulo aedium, in the open court, Liv 24, 16, 17.—Trop.: in propatulo, publicly (not in Cic. or Cæs.): pudicitiam in propatulo habere,offer it publicly, expose it to sale,: in propatulo esse, (with in promptu); cf. ; : statuas in propatulo abicit,.—
Abl.: propatulo, in the open air (postAug.): Mossyni propatulo vescuntur,.

la:verb:propello.gloss: to drive, push or urge forth or forward; hurl, propel
senses: to drive, push or urge forth or forward; hurl, propel
to hurl or cast down, overthrow, expel
to drive on, impel, incite, urge
to drive away, keep or ward off
la:verb:propello.html:
prō-pello (prŏpellat, ; ), pŭli, pulsum, 3, v. a.
Lit., to drive before one's self, to drive, push, or urge forward, to drive forth; to hurl, propel, hurl or cast down, to overthrow (class.; syn.: proturbo, protrudo): sacerdotem anum praecipem propulit,: oves potum,: in pabulum,: aëra prae se,: propellere ac submovere hostes,: hostem a castris,: nubes,: in profundum e scopulo corpora,: hastam,: urbem,to overthrow,: muros Oechaliae,to throw down,; cf.: orationem propellere dialecticorum remis,: si paulo largius L. Caecilium pietas et fraternus amor propulisset,.—
Trop.
To push or thrust forward (post-Aug.): cruda studia in forum,.—
To drive on, impel, incite, urge (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): corpus,: terrore carceris ad voluntariam mortem,: agmina voce,.—
To drive away, to keep or ward off: periculum vitae ab aliquo,: famem,: injurias hominum ac ferarum,.

la:noun:propagatio.html:
prō^pāgātĭo, ōnis, f.
1. propago
,
a propagating, propagation.
Lit. (class.): propagatio vitium,: propagationum genera tria sunt in usu maxime,: propagationes facere,.—
Transf.: quae propagatio et soboles origo est rerum publicarum, Cic. Off. 1, 17, 54.—
Trop.
An extending, prolonging; an extension, enlargement, prolongation (class.): finium imperii nostri propagatio,: miserrimi temporis,: vitae,: victoriam, triumphum, propagationem imperii portandi,. —
An establishing, honoring: nominis,.

la:noun:propolis.html:
prŏpŏlis, is, f., = πρόπολις,
the third foundation in making honey, a gummy substance with which the bees close the crevices of their hives, bee-glue, propolis: propolin vocant, quod apes faciunt ad foramen introitus protectum in alvum, maxime aestate,: prima fundamenta comosin vocant periti, secunda pissoceron, tertia propolin,; ; .

la:noun:propola.html:
prŏpōla (prōpōla, Lucil.
v.infra), ae, m., = προπώλης, a forestaller, a retailer, huckster (class.): sicuti cum primus ficos propola recentes protulit, Lucil. ap. ; : panis et vinum a propolā, atque de cupā,.— As adj., , n. 450.

la:noun:proportio.html:
prō-portĭo, ōnis, f.,
comparative relation, proportion, symmetry, analogy, likeness (class.): proportio, quod dicunt ἀνάλογον, Müll.; : Penatis singulariter Labeo Antistius posse dici putat, quia pluraliter Penates dicantur: cum patiatur proportio etiam Penas dici, ut optimas, primas, Antias, Fest. s. v. penatis, p. 253 Müll.: id optime assequitur quae Graece ἀναλογία, Latine (audendum est enim, quoniam haec primum a nobis novantur) comparatio, proportiove dici potest, ; and 9: uti proportione,; .

la:verb:propulso.html:
prōpulso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.
propello
,
to drive back, keep or ward off, to repel, repulse (class.).
Lit.: lupos,: hostem,: populum ab ingressione fori,: et aquas hiemis et vapores aestatis propulsare radicibus,; .—Absol.: ibi resistere ac propulsare,.—
Trop., to ward off, avert, repel: frigus, famem propulsare,: periculum capitis legum praesidio,: suspicionem a se,: bellum ab urbe ac moenibus,; : morbos exquisitis remediis,: violentiam vini,: praesidio vim propulsaturus,.

la:verb:propugno.html:
prō-pugno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
To rush out to fight, go forth to fight, to make sallies or sorties: ipsi ex silvis rari propugnabant,; cf. . 7; .—
To fight or contend for, to defend a thing (class.; syn.: tutor, defendo).
Lit.: uno tempore propugnare et munire,: pro suo partu,: multos e muris propugnantes hastā transfixit,. —
With dat. (post-class.): propugnare fratri,: puero misello,, p. 200, 13.—
Trop.: pro aequitate,: pro salute,.—With acc. (post-Aug.), to defend: absentiam suam,: dum quae libidine deliquerant, ambitu propugnant,; : pectora parmā,. 584; 4, 110.
la:verb:propugno.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

la:noun:propraetor.gloss: an ex-praetor (in Rome) sent as praetor to a province where there was no army
senses: an ex-praetor (in Rome) sent as praetor to a province where there was no army
la:noun:propraetor.html:
prō-praetor, ōris, m. (also prōprae-tōre or prō praetōre, indecl.),
a magistrate in the times of the republic, who, after having administered the prœtorship one year in Rome, was sent in the following year

as prœtor to a province where there was no army, a proprœtor (class.).—Form propraetor: cum bella a propraetoribus administrantur,.—Form pro praetore, : prorogatum Tubulo est, ut pro praetore in Etruriam succederet Calpurnio,.—

One who administers the prœtorship of a province in the absence of the prœtor: Aulo fratre in castris pro praetore relicto,: quem pro praetore in castris relictum supra diximus,; ; ; ; .

openly, publicly, notoriously, manifestly (class.): minus jam furtificus sum: rapio propalam,: signis propalam collocatis, * : dicere,: obviam ire,: alii propalam, alii per occultum,: propalam aspici,: timeo, ne hoc propalam fiat,may become manifest,: propalam est, it is clear, manifest (post-class.), P.

la:verb:propendeo.gloss: to hang down, forth or forward
senses: to hang down, forth or forward
to be inclined, disposed to, favourable
la:verb:propendeo.html:
prō-pendeo, di, sum, 2 (in , the correct reading is propendes), v. n.,
to hang forth or forward, hang down.
Lit. (class.): ex ramis propendens,; : lanx propendet,.—
Trop.
(The figure borrowed from the descending scale of a balance.) To weigh more, haec the preponderance: nec dependes nec propendes,weighest neither less nor more,: si bona propendent,.—
To be inclined or disposed to any thing: si suā sponte quo impellimus, inclinant atque propendent,, 44, 18.—
To be well disposed, favorable: inclinatione voluntatis propendere in aliquem,.—Hence, prō-pensus, a, um, P. a.
Lit., hanging down (post-class.): propensum labrum,: propenso sesquipede, dub. —
Transf., = magno pene praeditus (post-class.), .—
Trop.
Inclining towards, coming near, approaching (class.); with ad: disputatio ad veritatis similitudinem propensior,: ad veritatem,. —
Heavy, weighty, important (class.): illa de meā pecuniā ramenta fiat plumea propensior,: id fit propensius,more weighty, important,.—
Inclined, disposed, prone to any thing (syn. proclivis); usually constr. with ad or in and acc.; rarely with dat.
With ad: non tam propensus ad misericordiam, quam inclinatus ad severitatem videbatur,: ad dicendum,: animus propensus ad salutem alicujus,: ad liberalitatem,.—Comp.: paulo ad voluptates propensior,: ad lenitatem,: animus alius ad alia vitia propensior,: sunt propensiores ad bene merendum quam ad reposcendum,.—
With in and acc.: propensus in alteram partem,.—Comp.: propensior benignitas esse debebit in calamitosos,: in neutram partem propensiores,.—
With dat.: in divisione regni propensior fuisse Alexandro videbatur,more disposed to favor Alexander, (al. pro Alexandro).—
Absol., well-disposed, favorable, willing, ready (class.): propenso animo aliquid facere,; : propensum favorem petiit,.—Sup.: propensissimā civitatum voluntate, Auct. B. Alex. 26.—Hence, adv.: prōpensē, willingly, readily, with inclination (class.): conspiratio propense facta, Lentulus ap. .—Comp.: propensius senatum facturum,: eoque propensius laudandus est, Oud.

la:noun:propudium.html:
prō^pŭdĭum, ĭi, n.
pro-pudet
.
A shameful or infamous action (ante-class. and post-Aug.): propudium dicebant, cum maledicto nudare turpitudinem volebant, quasi porro pudendum. Quidam propudium putant dici, a quo pudor et pudicitia procul sint, Müll.: propudii aliquem insimulare,.—In plur.: hoc cinere poto propudia virorum inhiberi,.—
Transf., concr., a shameful person, vile wretch, a rascal, villain, a term of abuse (class.): quid ais, propudium?; ; cf. : propudium illud et portentum L. Antonius,; App M. 8, p. 215, 15.
